components.note: Vertices, edges, parents, directed paths of positive length, directed cycles including loops, acyclicity, descendants and topological order are all defined. The boundary n>=1 and the loop case are stated. The source's acyclicity, 'no directed cycles' (p. 110), is preserved. The source's kinship terms and undirected paths (p. 105) are defined on the route in def:p16-active-path.

The proof is written in full. The backward predecessor chain and the pigeonhole repeat give a cycle, which covers the loop case b=a+1. It then shows that acyclicity is preserved under removal, that exactly n removals occur for any choice of source vertex, and that the removal order is topological.

source_locators: Pearl 2009 pp. 103-104 (sec. 3.1: Wright, equation (2), exogenous variables and disturbances)
components.note: Present: the finite data; total functions; the S_empty and v_J conventions; exogenous disturbances that may be dependent; solutions; the assignment direction, which matches the source's equation (2) point; parent sets as the inputs a function may use; and an edge asserting no nonzero effect. components.gap: Preserve the source's structural interpretation that def:p16-finite-scm (body 51-87) omits, within the cited extent of secs. 3.1-3.2 (Pearl 2009, pp. 103-104 and 107). (a) Unobserved exogenous variables, the 'disturbances' or 'errors', represent factors omitted from the model but judged relevant to explaining the modelled variables. They are part of physical reality (e.g. genetic factors, socio-economic conditions) and are treated like any other variable, though often unmeasurable. They differ fundamentally from regression residuals, which are artifacts of analysis and by definition uncorrelated with the regressors (p. 104). (b) The historical claim that Sewall Wright (1921) first combined equations with a diagram whose arrows express the directionality of the assignment process and whose missing arrows make empirical claims (pp. 103-104). The entry renders this directionality point (body 81-85) without attribution. (c) The source's definition of the equations as 'structural' when they are autonomous, each function invariant to possible changes in the form of the others (Simon 1953; Koopmans 1953; p. 107). The chapter states this only as an unattributed invariance stipulation (body 121-125).

source_locators: Pearl 2009 p. 108 (equations (6)-(9), controlled distribution, causal effect)
components.note: Present: replacement of the equations in I by constants; preservation of Omega, q, the disturbances and the other equations; deletion of the incoming edges (Fig. 2(b)); the invariance stipulation; the definition corresponding to equation (7); the statement that no positivity is needed; events, intervention means, and the difference of means, which is equation (8).
components.gap: def:p16-causal-intervention (body 111-145) renders only the average difference, equation (8), from the source's presentation of the intervention operation (Pearl 2009, secs. 3.2-3.2.1, pp. 107-108). Supply the following in the finite formulation. (a) The experimental risk ratio E(Y|do(x0'))/E(Y|do(x0)), equation (9), with its nonzero-denominator boundary. (b) The variance Var(Y|do(x0)), and the source's statement that any other distributional parameter may enter the comparison, all of these being obtained from the controlled distribution P(Y=y|do(x)) = sum_z P(z,y|do(x)), which the source calls the 'causal effect'. (c) The source's reading of the post-intervention distribution (also called 'controlled' or 'experimental'), as distinguished from the pre-intervention distribution: the proportion of individuals that would attain each response and covariate level if treatment x0 were administered uniformly to the population (p. 108). (d) Two claims of p. 107. One is justificatory: extending SEM beyond linear models requires detaching 'effect' from a coefficient and redefining it as a general capacity to transmit changes among variables. The other is historical: the extension based on simulating hypothetical interventions was proposed by Haavelmo 1943, Strotz and Wold 1960, Spirtes et al. 1993, Pearl 1993a and 2000a, and Lindley 2002.

components.note: Every promised conclusion is proved in written steps. The intervened graph is a DAG, and the law exists, is unique and vanishes off v_I=x. Consistency is proved pointwise. Invariance of non-descendants is proved by the closure of H under parents and induction. The empty intervention and the order-independent composition of disjoint replacements are also proved. The source's 'sequential' interventions (p. 112) are covered by item 3.

components.gap: The statement and proof (body 218-241; annex 185-210) are complete. However, the source's examples and claims for the truncated factorization within the cited extent (sec. 3.2.3, pp. 111-112, and n. 8) are absent from the route. source_locators: Pearl 2009 p. 108 (identification question and parametric setting)
components.note: Present: the two-model criterion relative to a class with common observed coordinates; equality of laws; the nonidentification witness; and the separation of identification from estimation. The source's misprinted (10), which reads P(M1)=P(M1), is rendered with the intended P(M1)=P(M2).
components.gap: def:p16-causal-identification (body 246-262) gives the two-model criterion but omits the rest of the source's presentation of Definition 2 (Pearl 2009, pp. 108-109). (a) Its attribution to Pearl 2000a, p. 77. (b) The source's gloss: the details of M1 and M2 do not matter; the assumptions A (e.g. those encoded in the diagram) constrain the models so that equal P's entail equal Q's; and Q then depends on P only and should be expressible in terms of the parameters of P, that is, an identified quantity is a function of the observed law on the class. (c) The motivating contrast. In econometrics (Hurwicz 1950; Marschak 1950; Koopmans 1953) and social science (Duncan 1975; Bollen 1989), identification was usually posed in linear parametric settings as whether a parameter has a unique solution in terms of the parameters of P. Nonparametric causal quantities such as Q(M)=P(y|do(x)) have no parametric signature and are defined procedurally by simulating an intervention.

components.gap: def:p16-causal-chain (body 282-301) omits two items of the source's treatment of the Fig. 2(a) chain within the cited extent. (a) The third derived display of the p. 111 example: the distribution of Z is not affected by the intervention, P(z|do(x0)) = sum_y P(z)P(y|x0) = P(z). In finite form, summing k_Z(z)k_Y(y|x) over y gives k_Z(z) = P(Z=z). With it goes the source's remark that P(z) and P(y|x0) are the pre-intervention factors of (16). (b) The remark of sec. 3.2.2 (p. 109) that the coincidence E(Y|do(x0)) = E(Y|X=x0) of equations (11)-(13), and likewise P(y|do(x)) = P(y|x), rests on two assumptions only: Y is a function of X and U_Y alone, and U_Y is independent of (U_Z, U_X), hence of X. The example cites full mutual independence and does not preserve this weaker hypothesis variant. The exogenous-assignment argument of experimental-design-and-estimable-contrasts-w02b-p15-077.tex does not state the chain case.

components.note: The outcome space, weights, coordinate disturbances, equations and DAG are fully specified. The annex verifies normalization and the product form behind the asserted mutual independence. The common-cause reading is stated.

Every entry is computed: the table, the conditionals 5/8 and 3/8, the intervention probability 1/2 for both x, the mean differences 1/4 and 0, positive (X,Z) masses, the response factors 1/4 and 3/4, and the adjustment identity, each with explicit positive denominators.

Both witness pairs are constructed and checked. Item 1 uses M_A' with dependent disturbances against M_B with independent ones: the observational laws are equal and positive, and the targets are 1/2 and 5/8. Item 2 uses the singleton-outcome models M_C and M_D with independent constant disturbances: the observational laws are equal point masses, and the targets are 0 and 1.

This is the projection of the common-cause model onto X and Y with dependent disturbances. The warning shows the dependence (first coordinates agree with probability one) and that the constant kernels multiply to 1/4, which contradicts the proved table. The source's point that correlated errors arise from unmeasured confounders (p. 110) is rendered.

The procedure is given with its correctness and termination references: replacement, topological evaluation per outcome, and grouping. It gives the kernel/truncation alternative under independence, the positivity side condition for recovering kernels, the requirement to state the model class, and the limits of fitting a table. The source's p. 112 claim that truncated factorization bypasses equation manipulation is reflected in the second paragraph.
